Casing ahead of the excavation
The casing prevents the soil and groundwater from breaking in; in granular soil the casing must go ahead of the excavation. It is safe even in silty soil with a high water content.
Nothing to replace here
In this profile there is no groundwater along the bore, so the lack of water replacement causes no problem in the model. Try it in profile A, B or C!
Base failure!

The water removed from inside the casing is not replaced: because of the higher groundwater table outside (−${fmt(gw, 1)} m), water breaks in at the base and disturbs the soil – the base resistance drops significantly.
Water replacement in the bore
Below the groundwater table the water removed is replaced in the bore, so the soil does not break in at the base.
Bentonite slurry support
The slurry displaces the groundwater and supports the wall of the bore; the concrete is placed from the bottom up through a tremie pipe and displaces the slurry.
No groundwater along the bore
In this profile the drop in slurry level causes no collapse in the model – try it in profile A, B or C!

The slurry level has dropped close to the groundwater table (−${fmt(gw, 1)} m): the excess pressure is lost and the wall collapses. A discontinuity forms in the pile shaft, more concrete is needed, and the shaft resistance decreases.
Slurry level above the groundwater
The slurry level is kept well above the groundwater table throughout – this way the excess pressure on the wall of the bore is maintained.
A very long pile
In Hungarian practice a depth of 30–40 m is typically sufficient.
the groundwater (−${fmt(gw, 1)} m) is above the bottom of the bore

Without support the bore stands only in cohesive soil above the groundwater – here ${why.join(', és ')}. The result would be a discontinuity, more concrete and lower shaft resistance. Choose a casing, slurry or CFA!

Cohesive soil, above the groundwater
In hard cohesive soil above the groundwater the bore stands by itself for a short time – it must be concreted immediately after excavation.
Unsupported bore too deep
Without support work is done to a depth of at most 8–10 m – here ${fmt(L, 1)} m.
${fmt(L, 1)} m: an unsupported bore can be at most 8–10 m deep.
Excavated block foundation
Up to a depth of 5–6 m such a foundation is also called an excavated block foundation or well foundation.
Square pile too long
Square piles (30×30, 40×40 cm) are typically 4–12 m long. A longer one needs a round spun pile (max. 20–22 m).
Precast pile too long
Round spun piles are at most 20–22 m long.
In Hungarian practice the square pile is 30×30 or 40×40 cm.
The pile refuses!
In hard (stony) clay the precast pile cannot be driven to the design depth – here it stops at approx. −${fmt(M.stuck, 1)} m.
The pile refuses in the fill!
Pile driving cannot be used in fill with large blocks – a single thinner such layer can prevent the pile from getting down.
Displacement compacts
The driven pile pushes aside and compacts the soil around it: for a precast pile both the base and the shaft resistance increase.
Vibration-sensitive neighbour: the riskiest choice
Noise and vibration
Driving causes significant noise and vibration; near structures it can only be used under strict limits.
A bored (CFA) or screw pile is the better choice here.
Franki pile too long
The length of a Franki pile is at most approx. 16–18 m.
At the limit of the Franki pile length
It does not reach the bearing stratum
The casing is driven into the bearing stratum – that is where the bulb gives a high base resistance.
Widened base: the “bulb”
The rammed concrete bulb gives a high base resistance; a resistance of 2000–3000 kN can be achieved. In Hungary it has almost completely disappeared by now.
Driving, ramming
The casing is driven down with a drop hammer and the concrete is rammed – with dynamic effects and noise.
To be avoided next to a vibration-sensitive neighbour.
Screw pile too long
The length of a screw pile is at most approx. 20 m.
Not ideal in hard clay
The screw pile is popular and economical mainly in loose or medium-dense granular and intermediate, weakly cohesive soil.
Deep in the dense gravel
The displacement head progresses only with difficulty in a dense layer – the technology is for loose, medium-dense soil.
No vibration, hardly any spoil
While drilling, the head pushes aside and compacts the soil: the shaft resistance increases, little spoil comes to the surface, and there is no dynamic effect or noise.
Buckling!
In the ${weak.n} layer the undrained shear strength is below 10 kPa: the buckling of the slender micropile must be checked separately.
Only the shaft counts
For the resistance of a slender micropile the tip resistance is typically neglected. A resistance of 130–180 kN can be achieved with a hollow-bar grouted micropile.
Small rig, tight space
It can be used in places with difficult access and low headroom, and for underpinning an existing building.
Even next to a vibration-sensitive neighbour
Drilling is not dynamic; installing the casing by rotation is gentler than by vibration.
Making a bored pile involves no vibration from driving.
The neighbour doesn’t feel it either
There is no driving or vibrating while screwing.

The base is in the bearing stratum
The pile penetrates ${fmt(Lact - P.bear, 1)} m into the bearing stratum (−${fmt(P.bear, 1)} m).
No outstanding bearing stratum
There is no better layer near the base – the shaft of the longer pile does more of the work.
